strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Technology billionaires account for all of the USD 845 billion of new wealth made in 2026, Bloomberg finds, while fortunes built elsewhere are USD 62 billion poorer
lead.standfirst: Elon Musk now stands at USD 977 billion and Michael Dell has added USD 89.1 billion, in a ranking where the whole of the year's gain sits in a single industry.
lead.body:
Bloomberg's Billionaires Index, as reported on 5 October, shows that billionaires with technology fortunes account for the entire USD 845 billion of wealth gained so far this year. Billionaires whose fortunes sit outside technology are, taken together, USD 62 billion poorer over the same period. The year's gains have not been shared across the list. They have been collected by one sector.

At the top, Elon Musk is shown at USD 977 billion. Michael Dell added USD 89.1 billion to reach USD 229 billion, the second-largest dollar gain on the index after Mr Musk's. Bloomberg also flags signs that the surge may be nearing its peak, a caution worth holding beside the headline numbers. These are estimates of paper wealth that move with share prices every day, not cash in an account.

For the private service market, the significance lies in how the wealth is held. A fortune concentrated in the shares of one company is a different household from a diversified one. Its net worth can move by billions in a week, and liquidity tends to arrive in events, such as a sale of stock, a listing or a vesting date, rather than as a steady income. Decisions about houses, aircraft and staff can follow those events rather than the calendar.

Those who serve such families tend to see the effect in the diary before they see it in the headline. Purchases and hires can cluster around liquidity, and a principal whose wealth is tied to one company may also carry a public profile tied to that company, with the privacy and security questions that follow. The index is a measure of wealth. What it implies for a household is something the person running that household has to read for herself.
lead.why: A household's spending rhythm follows how its wealth is held, so a manager who understands concentration, liquidity events and public exposure can plan staffing, security and cash far better than one who reads only the headline net worth.
lead.src: Bloomberg Billionaires Index, via AI Weekly

articles.title: Jet card prices fell 3.1 per cent in the third quarter, the lowest reading since late 2023, even as the two largest business jet makers carry order books worth close to USD 46 billion
articles.body:
Private Jet Card Comparisons reported on 5 October that jet card rates fell 3.1 per cent in the third quarter, the lowest reading since the fourth quarter of 2023. Aviation International News, summarising the same data, reports rates down both from the previous quarter and from a year earlier, with the turboprop category leading the declines after the pause at OneFlight. In July the same index had shown rates up about half a point on the year but down about one point since the first quarter, so the softening has been building through 2026.

The pricing sits oddly beside the manufacturers' books. Forecast International's analysis of 7 August puts Bombardier's backlog at USD 21.8 billion at the end of the second quarter, up from USD 17.5 billion at the end of 2025, and Gulfstream's at USD 24.0 billion, up from USD 21.8 billion. Bombardier delivered 56 aircraft in the first half and guides to more than 157 for the year, while Gulfstream delivered 79 and guides to roughly 160. Both booked more than they delivered in the second quarter, with a book-to-bill ratio of 1.5 times at each.

The two trends are not contradictory. A jet card is a prepaid block of hours on someone else's fleet, so its price reflects charter supply, demand and the health of operators. A backlog reflects owners who want their own aircraft and will wait for it, and Forecast notes build cycles of 12 to 24 months at Bombardier. The likeliest reading is that a softer card market is a good moment to buy hours, while a full backlog shows that for some principals ownership remains the aim.

For whoever organises a family's flying, a cheaper quarter is an opening to compare and renegotiate, not a reason to read the contract less closely. The sharpest fall came in the category that followed a provider's pause, and a card is only as good as the operator standing behind it.
articles.why: Card pricing, operator health and aircraft waiting times are three separate dials, and the person who arranges a family's flying is the one expected to know which of them has moved before the next renewal.
articles.src: Aviation International News, Private Jet Card Comparisons, Forecast International

articles.title: A Beaune domaine reports red yields 50 to 70 per cent below normal on the first day of the 2026 harvest, and the cellar a house is buying for will hold fewer bottles
articles.body:
Bill Nanson's Burgundy Report diary for 24 August, the first day of picking at a domaine in Beaune, records yields well down. Reds are usually 50 to 70 per cent below normal and whites often down by as much as half. Bunches are consistently small, and there is, in his words, very little juice in them.

The cause given is water stress. Well-draining slope parcels suffered most, with many yellowing leaves, and even the lower alluvial parcels drained too freely this year. On quality, the early signs are kind: sorting needed little work, and the pinot noir was ripe but pure, with no prune or overdone notes at this stage. The domaine's head played down the difference between 13 and 15 hectolitres per hectare, provided the fruit has been well sorted. Thunder and heavy rain arrived that evening.

The caution is plain. This is one domaine on one day, and the report does not describe the vintage as a whole. Other growers and other appellations may have fared differently, and quality can only be judged once the wines are made. A start in late August is early for Burgundy by historical standards, and the diary should be read as a first signal, not a verdict.

What a short crop means for a cellar is a general principle of the trade. When volumes fall, domaines tend to allocate to long-standing customers, and the bottles go first to those who have kept the relationship. The person buying for a house is rarely the person with the best claim on a scarce allocation, unless she has built one.
articles.why: A short vintage rewards the cellar manager who holds allocations and relationships, so reading a harvest report from the vineyard is part of the work of buying for a house.

articles.title: Personal assistants draw about 112 applications per search and butlers about 48, yet roughly four in five candidates are turned down, Morgan & Mallet's 2026 report shows
articles.body:
Morgan & Mallet's Household Staff Industry Report 2026, updated in June, draws on more than 450,000 applications since 2016 across 70 countries and a network of more than 56,300 vetted professionals in over 100 roles. About four in five candidates assessed are turned down. The firm's reading is that the market suffers from a shortage of suitable candidates, not of candidates.

The applications per search show where the scarcity lies. Personal assistants attract about 112, chauffeurs about 106 and estate or house managers about 80, against about 48 for butlers, 46 for private chefs, 37 for nannies, 34 for housekeepers, 26 for governesses and 24 for domestic couples. The butler figure rests on more than 7,800 applications across 167 searches, from a network of 1,882 butlers of 38 nationalities, 90 per cent of them men. The estate and house manager network counts 2,314, around 80 per cent men, with about 17 years of experience on average.

The vetting is the part a candidate controls least and should expect most. It runs to a 90-minute structured interview before any presentation to a client, reference checks with former employers, employment verification going back five to seven years, and criminal background screening. The workforce it produces spans 124 nationalities and 91 languages, with an average age of 43. French nationals are the largest group, followed by Filipinos by a wide margin.

The figures are the firm's own records and are not independently verified, and the report itself sets aside demand growth by country because it tracks the agency's expansion rather than the market's. Within those limits, one detail stands out. Domestic couples show the longest tenure, at 4.2 years, and butlers the shortest listed, at 2.6.
articles.why: The funnel described here is the one a candidate will face in practice, a long interview and five to seven years of history that can be checked end to end, so the preparation that matters is a record that stands up to verification.
articles.src: Morgan & Mallet Household Staff Industry Report 2026

briefs.t: The art market grew 4 per cent in 2025 to USD 59.6 billion
briefs.b: The Art Basel and UBS report, published on 12 March, counts dealer sales of USD 34.8 billion and public auction sales of USD 20.7 billion, up 9 per cent. Auction sales above USD 10 million rose 30 per cent, while online sales fell 11 per cent to USD 9.2 billion. The United States holds 44 per cent of the market, the United Kingdom 18 per cent, China 14 per cent and France 8 per cent.
briefs.src: The Art Basel and UBS Global Art Market Report 2026

briefs.t: Only about a third of family offices have a clear succession plan
briefs.b: UBS's Global Family Office Report 2026, published on 28 May, surveyed 307 offices with an average net worth of USD 2.7 billion. Some 27 per cent are preparing the next generation in a structured way, and 65 per cent have invested across the AI value chain. Sixty per cent plan to adjust their strategic asset allocation within a year.
briefs.src: finews.com, UBS Global Family Office Report 2026

briefs.t: London sold 34 homes above GBP 15 million in six months, worth GBP 1.24 billion
briefs.b: Beauchamp Estates counts sales up 79 per cent in value on the first half of 2025, with an average price of GBP 36.5 million. American and Gulf buyers took 55 per cent of the deals, and two sales topped GBP 100 million, the largest at Providence House in Chelsea for GBP 275 million. The figures come from a single agency's survey.
